analysis.title: The Necessary and Sufficient Conditions for an End to the Iran War
key_insights: Trump's desire for an exit after the midterms is a necessary but not sufficient condition for ending the Iran War. Both sides must prefer settlement, there must be overlap in minimum terms, and a sequencing formula must resolve the commitment problem that made the Islamabad MoU fragile.
The main hurdles to a settlement are the level of strategic failure the Trump administration is willing to acknowledge and its capacity to manage a diplomatic process, not US voter preferences.
Tehran will likely read the midterm result as proof its war strategy worked, so it will maintain or harden its stance.

In October Iran attacked more ships in or around Hormuz than in any month since February. The aim is to offset rising oil shipments with higher global prices, which have been a central tool for deepening Trump's political troubles and deterring new US strikes. Attacks on shipping continued in the first days of November.

Markets now price a lower probability of US strikes after the midterms. This raises pressure on Iran as long as the US offers no diplomatic solution, because high oil prices are a key instrument of Iran's war strategy.

Pre-war US demands were full dismantlement of the nuclear program, significant limits on ballistic missiles, and an end to support for regional militias. Iran is unlikely to concede at that level. The best near-term US outcome is Hormuz traffic returning to near normal, with greater Iranian control and rents, plus possibly marginal nuclear concessions.

The Supreme Leader has listed the right to enrich uranium and possession of enriched uranium stocks as red lines, so nuclear progress will be difficult. VP Vance said in October he wanted something 'meaningful' from Iran on enrichment capacity.
Iran's economy faces substantial pressure (World Bank projects a 7.7% GDP contraction for 2026, IMF 7.6%), but the leadership may judge a strategic victory worth costs borne over generations.

Iran's more feasible demands are lifting the blockade, restoring oil waivers, releasing frozen assets (about USD 24bn in two installments was discussed in June), and lifting sanctions imposed after July 2026.

Harder Iranian demands are US reparations (likely a non-starter), a ceasefire on all fronts including Lebanon (Israel controls this and is unlikely to agree while Hezbollah is strong), and US recognition of the Iran-Oman designated Hormuz shipping route as the primary one.

The Houthis are fighting Saudi Arabia separately, pushing through Taiz toward Aden. They reportedly demand USD 51bn to halt hostilities and recognition as Yemen's rulers, per the WSJ. An all-fronts ceasefire would be hard to enforce.
Sequencing is a binding constraint. Iran wants frozen funds returned and the blockade (reimposed July 14) lifted first, with nuclear talks last. Vance says the sides must 'trade actions for actions.'

Iran wants guarantees that US concessions such as oil export sanction relief will be permanent. Trump's lame-duck status and a Democrat-controlled Congress from January 3, 2027 weaken the credibility of US commitments.

A constructive path would pair a first installment of frozen assets via Qatar and lifting of the blockade with an end to attacks on shipping and a reopening of Hormuz. Qatar has already shortened Iran's proposed reopening timeline from seven days to two.

Return of inspectors and elements of the JCPOA look low-probability given the hardline regime. Israel will likely oppose an arrangement that strengthens Iran, and the Houthis act independently of Iran.

Interim arrangements are more likely than a comprehensive deal. The more likely non-escalatory scenario is Hormuz transit converging toward pre-war levels as Iran extracts some rents, with only a limited set of its demands met, such as an end to the blockade and release of frozen assets.

Markets pricing lower escalation looks somewhat premature. Reports say the US military has plans to resume strikes after the midterms and Gulf allies were told to prepare. A weakened Trump who cannot get a sellable deal may opt for a short, sharp strike, and Iran may respond by absorbing strikes while keeping military pressure on the region, risking a wider phase.

tension_points.bull_case: The midterms strengthen Trump's motive to exit, and an interim deal could see Hormuz transit converge toward pre-war levels with the blockade lifted and frozen assets released, markets pricing lower escalation.
tension_points.bear_case: Iran reads the midterms as leverage and holds out, sequencing and credibility problems persist, and a weakened Trump who wants out but cannot get a sellable deal may order a short, sharp strike that triggers a wider phase.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Reports that US military plans to resume strikes after the midterms are carried out, or continued Iranian attacks on Hormuz shipping with no diplomatic progress.
